> 天長地久。天地所以能長且久者，以其不自生，故能長生。

For six chapters the book has been describing the Dao. Chapter 7 turns the camera around and points it at a person.

The argument takes three steps, and the third is where nearly every reading goes wrong.

## Step one: 不自生

Heaven and earth last because they do not live for themselves. 不自生 does not mean they abstain from existing; it means they are not organized around their own continuation.

A thing that exists in order to keep existing spends its capacity on its own maintenance. A thing that exists as the condition for other things to exist does not have that expense. The sky does not eat.

## Step two: 後其身而身先，外其身而身存

The sage imitates: put yourself behind, and you end up ahead; set yourself outside, and you are preserved.

These read like positioning tactics, and that is exactly the danger. Used as tactics, they work for a while and then curdle — the person who steps back in order to be advanced is still calculating, and everyone can feel the calculation.

The lines are better read as consequences, not methods. When your attention is genuinely occupied by the thing in front of you, you are not busy managing your rank; and because you are not busy managing it, it tends to settle. That is 身先 as an effect, not a maneuver.

## Step three: 非以其無私邪？故能成其私

This is the line that gets quoted in bad management books: be selfless and you'll get what you want.

Read carefully, the sentence has two different 私 in it. The first is the absence of private calculation — 無私. The second, 成其私, is not the same object: it is the private good that gets completed, not the private good that gets traded for.

The difference is the difference between giving something up and no longer needing to hold it. A person who drops the calculation does not thereby earn a payout; what happens is that the thing they would have been calculating about stops being scarce in the same way.

If the logic were exchange — sacrifice now, collect later — the chapter would be a manual for ambitious people, and 老子 would have written a much shorter and more popular book.

## What the two 私 actually are

The first 私 is the self treated as a center that everything else is measured against. The second is the self as one of the conditions in the situation — real, functioning, but not the axis.

Moving from the first to the second is not self-erasure. It is what makes 後身 and 外身 possible without performance: you can step back because the center is no longer the only place worth standing.

## A test

Think of the last time you did something well and then spent more energy protecting the credit than doing the work. That gap is 自生 — existence organized around its own continuation. It is also, usually, where the exhaustion lives.
